claim: A second-order generalized-Maxwell tissue model identified from a bounded pre-touch supports practical offline force-controller tuning for sheep spinal-cord contact, but does not establish online adaptation, optimal impedance selection, or safety under heterogeneous continuous sliding.
epistemic_status: Author-reported modeling and experiments; novelty and residual-gap implications are bounded reader inferences.
problem_and_setting: Force-servo control in robot-assisted laminectomy near sheep spinal cord and dura, balancing representation of stress relaxation against repeated-simulation cost.
method_or_mechanism: One elastic element is placed in parallel with n Maxwell units. Differential evolution identifies order and parameters from one safe pre-touch trajectory at 100 Hz with displacement limited to 3 mm. The selected second-order transfer function supports offline loss-based tuning of PID, LADRC, and IMC.
content_summary: One Maxwell unit misses force decay, while two units reportedly capture the trend to the noise level. Higher order improves fit but raises simulation cost. A 10-s simulation takes 140.8±5.6 ms; measured optimization times are about 4.5 s for IMC, 16.2 s for PID, and 32.3 s for LADRC. Sheep-spine step tests show similar overall performance, with smaller PID overshoot, greater LADRC noise sensitivity, and slight IMC benefit. The workflow remains offline-calibrated without clinical cohort or formal safety certificate.
synthesis_role: Direct prior for low-order viscoelastic tissue identification plus controller tuning; it excludes novelty based only on fitting a generalized-Maxwell model and using it for force control.
development_link: Use the second-order model and offline-tuned controllers as baselines; retain online relaxation, heterogeneity, or sliding state only if it changes optimal impedance actions and held-out safety/task outcomes after geometry, material, speed, direction, or history shifts.

evidence.finding: An elastic element plus n Maxwell units is identified by differential evolution from one pre-touch trajectory sampled at 100 Hz and limited to 3 mm.
First order misses force decay; second order captures the reported trend, while higher orders increase simulation time.
A 10-s simulation takes 140.8±5.6 ms and measured optimization takes about 4.5 s IMC, 16.2 s PID, and 32.3 s LADRC.
Three optimized controllers perform similarly; PID may overshoot less, LADRC is noisier, and IMC gains slightly from the internal model.
Direction or angle changes may require recalibration; online adaptation needs more compute; nonlinearity, temperature sensitivity, tactile feedback, and broader clinical tests remain unresolved.
The study supports a low-order calibrated compromise but does not show state identifiability or action relevance during changing sliding contact.

boundary_conditions: Force steps rather than continuous sliding
No universal force limit, passivity, or chance guarantee
assumptions: Linear generalized-Maxwell dynamics hold in the tested range
Calibration remains valid in later control
Geometry and tissue state remain near calibration

reported: Online adaptation and broader clinical validation are unresolved
inferred: Offline parameters may fail under heterogeneity, sliding, or history
Similar controller performance questions action relevance of added detail
Good tracking does not establish injury safety
Unused online state complexity would be unjustified

conflicts_with: Novelty from low-order viscoelastic identification plus force-controller tuning
Adequacy of a single relaxation mode
Safety generalization beyond calibrated sheep-spine steps

problem_lead_search_contexts.lead_statement: Hunt-Crossley may be an inadequate environment model for optimal impedance when soft contact exhibits decision-relevant relaxation, creep, hysteresis, or rate history that cannot be represented by current penetration and penetration rate alone.
problem_lead_search_contexts.purpose: Attempt to disconfirm the adequacy of memoryless Hunt-Crossley contact by locating direct soft-tissue force-control evidence for relaxation, creep, hysteresis, or frequency dependence and the control consequences of including or omitting memory.
problem_lead_search_contexts.expected_close_condition: Establish whether history-dependent viscoelasticity causes a measurable, decision-relevant control failure in the target regime and define the rate/hold conditions under which Hunt-Crossley remains sufficient.
